note: All numbers are model confidences (0 to 1), not versions. Jev = jev-1.14.0. Laya = laya-multilingual, max_len 8192, not truncated. Both are second opinions on design questions only, never verifiers; zero-shot Laya is uncalibrated.

state.decision: Design decisions for GrapiX, a professional real-time broadcast graphics suite for live esports and sports TV, raised by an external design review of the wireframes.
state.product: GrapiX has an Editor (design studio, never live, cannot put anything on air) and Playout (the only application that takes, cues or clears graphics on air). Operators are live-broadcast crews; designers are motion graphics professionals who know After Effects and Ross XPression. The Editor shows parts, a stage and one selected-part card with Look, Motion and Data sections, each with a More button for advanced properties. Animation is organised into four moments: Appears, Stays, Changes, Leaves; Moments are a simple front over keyframes and a Fine-tune button opens keyframes and curves. The engine is frame-exact and the sole clock. Scene logic runs in a per-scene sandbox with a JS editor and a node view that share one vocabulary of actions and events. Layouts are named, saved files with light docking. The Editor has six menus plus Ctrl K command search. A scene has a Scene ID shared by Editor and Playout, automatic from 1 and editable, with takes referencing the scene by an internal key; a Take ID exists only in Playout, typed by the operator and unique. In Playout the word Cued already means a scene preloaded in preview. Names are working titles kept in one terms table.
state.review_summary: An external review says: keep a full professional timeline beside a simple Motion Builder, both on one animation model; use an expandable Inspector; use ten menus and named workspaces (Design, Animation, Effects, Data, Logic); give Scene an immutable internal ID plus an editable display ID; make live field updates configurable per field; build JavaScript scene logic first and nodes later; let the Editor control the field schema and Playout control the values; keep established broadcast terms (Take, Take ID, Preview, Program) and rename only where it helps.

timeline.instructions: How should motion authoring be offered to professional designers?

criteria.A: Moments only; keyframes stay hidden behind a Fine-tune button.
criteria.B: A full timeline as a first-class view beside the simple Moments view, both editing the same keyframes so a preset becomes editable keyframes and custom curves are never overwritten.
criteria.C: A full timeline only, with no Moments view.

inspector.instructions: How should the properties of the selected part be presented?

criteria.A: One card with Look, Motion and Data sections; advanced properties under More buttons.
criteria.B: An expandable inspector with property categories, tabs and a searchable full property list.

menus.instructions: Which menu structure suits a professional graphics application that also has Ctrl K command search?

criteria.A: Six menus (File, Edit, Graphic, Publish, View, Help) plus command search.
criteria.B: About ten menus (File, Edit, Scene, Object, Motion, Effects, Data, View, Window, Help) plus command search.

workspaces.instructions: How should panel arrangements be handled?

criteria.A: Every module is available at once through toggles and named saved layouts; no workspace restricts any tool.
criteria.B: Fixed named workspaces (Design, Animation, Effects, Data, Logic) that designers switch between, each a saved panel arrangement.

scene_id.instructions: What should the Scene ID rule be?

criteria.A: One Scene ID, automatic from 1 and editable, shared by Editor and Playout; takes reference the scene by an internal key so renaming it is safe.
criteria.B: An immutable auto-generated internal ID that all references use, plus a separate editable display identifier.

live_fields.instructions: How should live data updates to an on-air graphic be governed?

criteria.A: Every published field updates live in the same way once the take is verified.
criteria.B: Each published field is configured as live-updating or locked, with validation rules, so score and timer fields update without re-preview while others require a new take.

criteria.A: JavaScript first, nodes later, sharing one vocabulary of actions and events.
criteria.B: A node view first, JavaScript later.
criteria.C: Both at once in the first version.

schema_values.instructions: Who controls what for published fields?

criteria.A: The Editor controls the field schema (names, types, limits, permissions); Playout controls the values.
criteria.B: Playout can also add or change fields.

take_word.instructions: What should happen to the established words Take, Take ID, Preview and Program, given Playout already uses Cued for preloaded?

criteria.A: Keep Take, Take ID, Preview and Program as they are.
criteria.B: Rename Take to Cue and Take ID to Cue ID.

naming_principle.instructions: What naming principle should GrapiX follow?

criteria.A: Rename most standard design and broadcast terms to create a product identity.
criteria.B: Keep standard design and broadcast terms and give distinct names only to signature features.

agree_with_external_review: take_word (both keep Take / Take ID: Laya 0.95, Jev 1.0)
disagree_between_models: timeline: Jev B (full timeline beside Moments, same keyframes), confidence 1.0; Laya picked C with only 0.39, effectively undecided
inspector: Jev B expandable inspector (0.70); Laya A single card (0.62)
scene_id: Jev B immutable internal ID plus editable display ID (0.96); Laya A (0.50, a coin toss)
live_fields: Jev B configurable per field (1.0); Laya A (0.74)
logic_first: Jev A JavaScript first (1.0); Laya B nodes first (0.41, weak)
reading.my_reading: Where Jev is confident and Laya is near 0.5 (timeline, scene_id, logic_first) I treat Jev as the signal; both models are weak on the inspector and live_fields split, so those are decided by evidence in the verification report, not by either model.
